name: People and roles
about: Each of these people sees a different site.
lenses: Lapsed user coming back after a long gap
Parent or guardian acting for a child
Sceptic looking for reasons not to trust it
Account owner versus invited team member
Recruiter judging the people who built it
Teacher using it as an example
Freelancer or agency quoting to rebuild it
Successor who inherits it years later

name: Situations, devices and contexts
about: The same person gets a different site depending on where and how they open it.
lenses: Feature phone or proxy browser (Opera Mini)
Old operating system that cannot update its browser
Split-screen or a narrow resized window
Use in a noisy place with sound off
Use in a quiet place where sound would embarrass
Use at work on a monitored network
Use on a shared family computer
Use on a borrowed or public device
Use behind a corporate firewall or proxy
Use from a country the site did not plan for
In-app browser (opened from Instagram, WhatsApp, Facebook)
Browser extensions that rewrite the page
Bookmarking and returning via deep link
Many tabs of the same site open at once
Returning after the session has expired
Arriving by typing the address from memory
Arriving on a deep page, never seeing the home page

name: Experience and usability
about: These judge how the site feels and works for a person trying to get something done.
lenses: Clarity of purpose (what is this and who is it for?)
User goals and jobs to be done
User journey from arrival to goal
Wayfinding (where am I, where can I go?)
Mental models (does it work the way people expect?)
Signifiers (what hints at how to use it?)
Feedback (does the site confirm what I did?)
User control and freedom (undo, cancel, back)
Decision fatigue and number of choices
Service design (the whole service around the site)

name: Moments, states and flows
about: Every part of a site has moments where it can succeed or fail on its own.
lenses: First success (the moment the product proves itself)
Saving for later, wishlists and favourites
Edge cases: huge lists and large numbers
Edge cases: odd characters and emoji
Edge cases: missing images or data
Edge cases: two people editing at once
Edge cases: the first and the ten-thousandth item
SMS and WhatsApp messages the site sends
What happens to an account when its owner dies

name: Accessibility and inclusion
about: These ask who is shut out, and why.
lenses: Blind users with a screen reader
Deafblind users with a braille display
Users with one hand or a temporary injury
Users with speech differences using voice input
Situational limits (bright sun, holding a baby, noisy room)
Focus management in dialogs and after page changes
Link text that makes sense out of context
Accessible names for buttons and icons
Colour contrast of controls and graphics
Screen-reader compatibility across products (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack)
Name inclusivity (single names, long names, non-Latin names)
Address and phone formats beyond one country
Local currency, units, dates and number formats
Affordability of data needed to use it
Affordability of the device needed to use it
Access without a bank card, email address or smartphone
Access without a fixed address or ID document

name: Visual design
about: These judge the site as something seen.
lenses: Photography quality and authenticity (stock versus real)
Image cropping and art direction across screen sizes
Component states (default, hover, active, focus, disabled)
Personality and tone of the visuals
Trend-following and how it will date
Art-critical view (the site as an object of its era)
Skeuomorphic, flat, material, brutalist or other style schools

name: Content and language
about: These judge what the site says and how it says it.
lenses: Claims and whether they can be backed
Rhetoric (how it argues and whom it addresses)
Semiotics (what its signs and metaphors mean)
Naming of products, features and plans
Content for different stages of the buying journey
Content for different audiences on one site
What is missing that visitors expect to find

name: Front end
about: These look at what the browser receives and runs.
lenses: Preprocessors and build steps for styles
Rendering strategy (server, client, static, incremental, streaming)
Form handling and validation on the client
Client storage: local and session storage
Icons and how they are delivered
Browser APIs used (geolocation, camera, clipboard, share)
Internationalisation plumbing in the front end
Accessibility tree produced by the markup
Email HTML (a separate front end with its own rules)

name: Back end and data
about: These look at what happens on the server and in the data.
lenses: Name, address and phone data formats
Master data and single source of truth
Data warehouse or lake feeding from the site
Machine-learning models used by the site
Mainframes, spreadsheets or manual steps hidden behind the interface

name: Architecture, infrastructure and operations
about: These look at where the site lives and how it is kept running.
lenses: Separation of front end and back end
Hosting model (shared, VPS, dedicated, cloud, on-premises)
Recovery time and recovery point targets
Cost per user or per request
Dependency on external services (payment, maps, auth)
What happens when each external service fails

name: Code and engineering health
about: These judge the code as something people must live with.
lenses: Time for a new developer to make a first change
Decision records (why things are the way they are)
Ownership of each part of the code
AI-assisted or AI-generated code and how it was reviewed
Contribution to or dependence on open source
Conway's law (how the team's structure shows in the code)

name: Performance and reliability
about: These ask how fast the site is and how often it fails.
lenses: Core Web Vitals as a set
Performance of the first visit versus repeat visits
Font loading and flash of unstyled text
Sustainability: data transfer and device lifespan

name: Security
about: These ask what could go wrong on purpose.
lenses: Attacker's view (what is worth stealing or breaking?)
Account recovery as a weak point
Account enumeration (does the site reveal who has an account?)
Broken access control (seeing other people's data by changing an ID)
Exposed source maps, backups or config files
Supply-chain attacks on packages and build tools
Social engineering of staff and support
Staff access controls and least privilege
Security of mobile apps and APIs that share the back end
Security of admin and staff devices

name: Privacy, trust and safety
about: These ask what the site knows about people and how it protects them from each other.
lenses: Whether each item is needed (data minimisation)
Who inside the organisation can see it
Data sold or shared for advertising
Global Privacy Control and Do Not Track signals
Visibility of profiles and activity to other users
Data subject rights (access, correction, deletion, portability)
Use of user data to train AI

name: How machines see it
about: These look at the site as software reads it, which is often very different from what a person sees.
lenses: Expertise, experience, authority and trust signals
Search engines other than Google (Bing, DuckDuckGo, Yandex, Baidu)
Social link previews (Open Graph, Twitter cards)
Usability by AI agents acting for users
Scraper's view (how easily can data be extracted?)
Anti-bot measures from the bot's side
Accessibility tree read by assistive technology
Browser extensions that read the page
Spam-filter treatment of the domain's emails

name: Business, marketing and commerce
about: These ask what the site is for and whether it earns its keep.
lenses: Substitutes (what people use instead of the site)
Message match between advert and page
Local payment habits (EFT, mobile money, cash on delivery)
Returns policy as a selling point
Operational efficiency the site creates or destroys
Opportunity cost (what it should stop doing)
Non-profit and public-value measures (reach, impact, equity)

name: Measurement and research
about: These are the ways of finding out what is true about the site.
lenses: Data literacy of the people reading the reports
Contextual inquiry (watching people in their own setting)
Sales and support staff as sources
Reviews and social media as evidence

name: Legal, compliance and governance
about: These ask what rules apply and who answers for them. The laws named are examples; which ones apply depends on where the site and its users are.
lenses: Information officer or data protection officer registration
Electronic transactions law (ECTA in South Africa)
Disclosure of sponsored content and affiliate links
Copyright in the site's own content
Employment law for content about staff
Contracts with hosting and software vendors
Company information that must be displayed
Professional or industry codes of conduct
Ownership of the site and its accounts
Who holds the domain, hosting and admin log-ins
Content governance (who may publish and approve)
Dispute resolution and ombud routes for users

name: The organisation and process behind the site
about: A site reflects the people and habits that produce it.
lenses: Who owns it day to day
Handover quality between teams or suppliers
Deadlines and their effect on quality
Decision-making by evidence or by seniority
Feedback loop from users to the team
Feedback loop from support to the team
Change management for staff affected by the site
Diversity of the team and its blind spots
Labour conditions of those who build, moderate and maintain it
What would happen if the organisation closed tomorrow

name: Lenses specific to types of site
about: Each kind of site brings its own questions on top of the general ones.
lenses: Brochure site: does it explain the organisation and prompt contact?
Portfolio: does the work speak before the words do?
Personal site or CV: what does it say about the person?
News site: speed, accuracy, corrections, paywall
Magazine or long-form site: reading experience
Online shop: catalogue, basket, checkout, fulfilment
Marketplace: balance between buyers and sellers
Classifieds: trust, scams, freshness of listings
Travel site: search, price changes, hidden fees
Restaurant or venue site: menu, hours, location, booking
Property site: listings, maps, lead quality
Jobs site: search, applications, employer quality
Bank or finance site: security, clarity, regulation
Insurance or comparison site: neutrality and disclosure
Government service: reach, clarity, completion for everyone
Health site: accuracy, privacy, clinical safety
School or university site: parents, students, staff, admissions
School management system: records, timetables, reports, parent access
Dashboard or reporting tool: data clarity and trust in the numbers
Admin panel or back office: speed and error prevention for staff
Open-source project site: getting started, contribution
Social network: feed, identity, moderation, virality
Anonymous platform: safety, abuse, de-anonymisation risk
Forum or community: culture, moderation, archive value
Messaging or chat web app: reliability, privacy, presence
Music or podcast platform: playback, licensing, discovery
Photo or art site: image quality, rights, presentation
Game or interactive experience: fun, performance, controls
Gambling site: harm prevention and regulation
Adult site: age checks, consent, safety
Wiki or knowledge base: accuracy, editing, vandalism
Search engine or directory: relevance and bias
Crowdfunding or donation site: trust, transparency, payment
Charity or non-profit site: impact story, giving flow
Campaign or political site: persuasion, data use, disclosure
Religious or community organisation site: belonging, events, giving
Landing page: one message, one action
Microsite: lifespan and what happens after the campaign
Link-in-bio page: speed and clarity on mobile
Web tool or calculator: correctness of the result
Scraper or data dashboard: source reliability and legality
AI product or chatbot site: accuracy, safety, limits disclosure
Crypto or web3 site: wallet safety, scams, irreversibility
Internet-of-things or device control panel: safety of real-world actions
Remote-control or admin tool: what damage a wrong click can do
Archive or museum site: preservation, citation, rights
Library or catalogue: search and metadata
Legal or professional services site: credibility and compliance
Medical practice site: booking, privacy, trust
Local business site: found on maps, opening hours, phone number
Multilingual or multi-country site: consistency versus local fit
Franchise or multi-brand site: shared system, separate identities
Web version of a native app: parity and hand-off
Browser extension or embedded widget: behaviour inside other people's sites
Email newsletter archive: readability outside the inbox
Parked, abandoned or zombie site: risk and reputation

name: Academic and theoretical disciplines
about: Any field of study can be pointed at a website.
lenses: Jakob's law (people expect sites to work like other sites)
Pragmatics (what is implied, not just said)
Architecture (space, flow, wayfinding as a metaphor)
Urban planning (public squares, private rooms, traffic)
Industrial design (the site as a product)
Film and motion theory (pacing, cuts, staging)
Graph theory (the site as nodes and edges)
Game theory (how users and the site outplay each other)
Ethnography (how people really use it in their lives)
Criminology (how it enables or deters crime)
Ethics: consequences (who is helped or harmed?)
Ethics: duties and rights (is anyone used merely as a means?)
Ethics: virtue (what character does it encourage?)
Philosophy of technology (does the tool shape the user?)
Epistemology (how does it shape what people believe?)
Phenomenology (what is it like to be on it?)
Critical theory (whose interests does it serve?)
Postcolonial critique (whose defaults are treated as universal?)
Marxist or labour critique (who does the work, who takes the value?)
Education and pedagogy (does it teach well?)
History (the site as a primary source)
Theology and religious studies (ritual, community, authority online)
Complexity science (emergent behaviour of many users)

name: Society, culture and the wider world
about: These look past the screen at what the site does in the world.
lenses: Gig work and labour it organises
Global North versus Global South defaults
Cultural assumptions built into forms and flows
Humour and idiom that do not travel
Dependence on a few technology companies
Colonial patterns in data and labour
Tax and where the profit lands
Effect on attention and mental health
Effect on body image and self-worth
Effect on sleep and time use
Effect on creative work and creators' income
Effect on language and how people write
Norms and etiquette the site creates
Communities and subcultures that form on it
Memes and shared references it spreads
Rituals of use (morning check, endless scroll)
Hardware demand and e-waste it drives
Water and land use of data centres
Use during protests, conflicts and shutdowns
Use by the vulnerable and the desperate
Dependence created (what breaks if it disappears?)
Public infrastructure role (has it become a utility?)
Commons and openness (does it give back to the web?)
Interoperability with the rest of the web
Link economy (does it link out or trap visitors?)
Contribution to web standards and health
What a fair-minded outsider would say about it
What its users would say if nobody from the company were listening

name: Time: past, present and future
about: A site is a moving thing, and each point in time shows something different.
lenses: Origin story (why it was first built)
Features that were removed and why
Old URLs and whether they still work
How well earlier versions have aged
Current lifecycle stage (new, growing, mature, declining)
Signs of neglect (dead links, old dates, expired certificates)
Daily and weekly rhythm of use
Peak moments (launches, sales, exam time, year end)
How long a relationship with a user lasts
Speed of change (daily releases or frozen for years)
Upcoming law or platform changes that will affect it
Scalability for the next ten times growth
Portability of content to a future system
Effect of AI on how people will reach and use it
Longevity (will it exist in ten years?)
What happens to user data at shutdown
Domain expiry and who might take it over
How a historian would read it in fifty years
What it will be remembered for
